name: Cervicogenic Headache
summary: Cervicogenic headache is a headache that arises from a problem in the neck, usually the upper cervical joints (C0–C3) or related structures. Pain from these areas can be felt in the head because the upper cervical nerves and the trigeminal system share connections in the brainstem.

looksLike: Usually one-sided headache, starting at the back of the neck or head and spreading forward.
Brought on or worsened by neck movement or sustained neck postures.
Neck stiffness or ache with the headache.
Not typically throbbing with nausea and light sensitivity (these point more toward migraine), though overlap can occur.
redFlags: Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion or rash
Neck pain or headache with dizziness, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, balance loss
New headache after age 50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision change
Progressive neurological deficit, personality change, new seizure
Cancer history, weight loss, night sweats
firstSteps: Initial approach: education plus manual therapy and exercise.
Justifying findings: one-sided neck-origin headache, neck triggers, reduced flexion-rotation, familiar response on palpation.
Priority: exercise and education, with manual therapy as an adjunct.

assess: Blood pressure and general neurological screen where available.
Posture and active neck movements; note range and headache response.
Palpation of the upper cervical joints for a familiar headache response.
Deep neck flexor endurance (craniocervical flexion test, if trained).
Cranial nerve and cervical neurological screen if indicated.

tests.name: Flexion-rotation test (FRT)
tests.purpose: Check mobility of the C1–C2 segment, where most neck rotation occurs when the neck is fully flexed
tests.positive: Clearly reduced rotation on one side compared with the other side and with published reference values, often with the familiar headache

measures: Record at each visit: headache frequency (days per week), intensity (0–10), duration, flexion-rotation range both sides, active neck movement, and a disability measure such as the Headache Disability Inventory or Neck Disability Index.

blocks.text: **Cervicogenic headache** is a headache that arises from a problem in the neck, usually the upper cervical joints (C0–C3) or related structures. Pain from these areas can be felt in the head because the upper cervical nerves and the trigeminal system share connections in the brainstem [Ref – to verify]. This is the accepted explanation, but the exact source of pain differs between patients.
It is a **working diagnosis** made from the history and exam. No single test confirms it, and it overlaps with migraine and tension-type headache.

items: Usually one-sided headache, starting at the back of the neck or head and spreading forward.
Brought on or worsened by neck movement or sustained neck postures.
Reduced neck movement, often rotation.
Neck stiffness or ache with the headache.
Not typically throbbing with nausea and light sensitivity (these point more toward migraine), though overlap can occur.

blocks.text: **Defer:** neck manipulation, strong end-range techniques and testing until the red flag is clarified.

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency red flag? **Yes:** emergency action.
Any urgent red flag? **Yes:** urgent referral, defer treatment.

One-sided headache starting in the neck, triggered by neck movement or posture, with reduced upper cervical rotation (flexion-rotation test) and a familiar-headache response to upper cervical palpation? **Yes:** working diagnosis is cervicogenic headache.
Features of migraine or tension-type headache dominate? **Yes:** treat as a mixed or alternative picture and involve the physician if unclear.

rows: C1–C2 self-SNAG or Mulligan SNAG (sustained natural apophyseal glide)
Aims to improve rotation without provoking headache [Ref – to verify]
Patient sits. A towel or strap held at C2 gives a gentle forward glide while the patient actively rotates the neck
Dizziness, headache increases, any neurological symptoms
May reduce headache frequency in the short term [Ref – to verify]
Reduced upper cervical mobility with a familiar response
Supine, gentle oscillations at C1–C3, low grade
Reduces stiffness that adds to neck load

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** gentle upper cervical mobilization or SNAG (as above), combined with exercise. Evidence suggests that manual therapy plus exercise can help, but it is moderate at best and short-term [Ref – to verify]. Avoid high-velocity upper cervical manipulation in a patient with headache and possible vascular features. The risk to benefit balance is debated and the screen should be thorough.
**Is it working?** Look for improved rotation on the flexion-rotation test, fewer headache days, and less intense headaches.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Lying, nod gently as if saying yes, hold
Can hold with no jaw or neck gripping
Sitting, draw shoulder blades back and down
Sitting, gentle side-bend and chin tuck
Short work breaks, gentle movement every 30 minutes

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** a mild ache that settles is acceptable. A headache that builds during an exercise, or dizziness, means stop.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 35-year-old office worker has a right-sided headache that starts at the base of the skull after long computer work. Right neck rotation is limited. Flexion-rotation range is clearly lower on the right than on the left, and C1–C2 palpation reproduces the familiar headache. No nausea, no aura, no red flags.
**Working diagnosis:** cervicogenic headache. **Plan:** education, C1–C2 self-SNAG, chin tuck, scapular training, workstation changes, reassess in two weeks.

items: Why compare the flexion-rotation test between sides? The test looks at the specific segment, and a clear side difference helps show a mobility problem. It does not prove the cause.
Why check for migraine features? Migraine can look similar, and treatment and referral differ.
Headache suddenly becomes the worst of the patient's life during an exam. What do you do? Stop immediately and call emergency services. This is a possible bleeding event.
Why avoid upper cervical manipulation in some patients? Because possible vascular warning signs should be excluded first, and the risk-benefit balance is debated.

Pressure on the neck is tender in a healthy volunteer. Why is tenderness alone not diagnostic? Because neck structures are often tender without disease. The reproduction of the familiar headache is more useful.
**Initial approach:** education plus manual therapy and exercise.
**Justifying findings:** one-sided neck-origin headache, neck triggers, reduced flexion-rotation, familiar response on palpation.
**Priority:** exercise and education, with manual therapy as an adjunct.
**Manual therapy:** C1–C2 SNAG or gentle mobilization, thoracic mobilization.
**Exercise:** chin tuck, scapular training, posture endurance.
**Modalities:** optional comfort only.
**Tell the patient:** the neck is a likely contributor, movement and exercise help, report sudden severe headache.
**Avoid:** manipulation without screening; techniques that provoke dizziness.
**Measure:** headache days, intensity, flexion-rotation, disability scale.
**If no improvement:** reconsider headache type; involve physician.
**Referral triggers:** red flags in Section G.
**Discharge:** headache controlled and self-management in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no red flags, clear mechanical neck link.

items: **Can be tested:** whether the flexion-rotation test separates cervicogenic headache from other headache types; whether manual therapy plus exercise reduces headache days.
**Hypotheses:** that C1–C2 techniques act by changing nociceptive input from the upper cervical spine.
**Future questions:** which patients benefit most, and the best dose.

blocks.text: Evidence strength is not graded until references are verified.
